extracted.intended_audience: students of Math 216 / graduate or advanced undergraduate readers learning foundations of algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, examples, and exercises concerning types of morphisms of schemes (finite, integral, finite type, finite presentation, quasi-finite, closed embeddings, etc.), and foundational results about images (Chevalley) and elimination theory. Intended as material for learning and exercising scheme-theoretic morphism concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is finite when on affines Spec A → Spec B the map B → A makes A a finitely generated B-module. Intuitively: think of finite as being closed plus finite fibers (though this isn’t quite true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties and remarks: finite morphisms are finite type and integral; images of closed sets are closed (Exercise 7.3.M; second proof in 8.2.5); finite morphisms have finite fibers (Exercise 7.3.K); composition of finite morphisms is finite (Exercise 7.3.I). Examples: branched covers Spec k[t] → Spec k[u] given by u = p(t); closed embeddings Spec A/I → Spec A; normalization maps (example to a nodal curve). Visualization: finite maps can be pictured as finite unions of points over Spec k (Example 7.3.H). Exercises include showing finite morphisms to Spec k yield finite discrete spectra with finite residue fields, and 'FINITE MORPHISMS TO Spec A ARE PROJECTIVE' (Exercise 7.3.J).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is integral if it is affine and the induced ring maps B → A (on affines) are integral ring morphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affine-local condition; closed under composition (Exercise 7.2.C). Integral morphisms are closed maps: images of closed sets are closed (Exercise 7.3.M). Finite morphisms are integral (Corollary 7.2.2), but the converse need not hold (counterexample referenced: Spec Q → Spec Q). Integral property is preserved by base change (Exercise 9.4.B(e)). Note: integral morphisms need not have finite fibers (7.3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally of finite type / finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: π : X → Y is locally of finite type if for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y and every affine open Spec A ⊂ π^{-1}(Spec B) the induced map B → A expresses A as a finitely generated B-algebra. A morphism is of finite type if it is locally of finite type and quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent affine-local formulation: π^{-1}(Spec B) can be covered by affines Spec A_i with each A_i a finitely generated B-algebra. Examples: the structure morphism P^n_A → Spec A is of finite type. Properties: open embeddings are locally of finite type; composition of (locally) finite type morphisms is (locally) finite type (Exercises 7.3.Q); if X and Y are locally Noetherian relevant simplifications apply. Use this to translate older notion 'scheme of finite type over k' as special case (5.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite presentation / locally of finite presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A B-algebra A is finitely presented if A ≅ B[x1,...,xn]/(r1,...,rj) (finite number of generators and finite number of relations). A morphism π : X → Y is locally of finite presentation if on affine opens the induced algebras are finitely presented. A morphism is of finite presentation if it is locally of finite presentation and quasiseparated and quasicompact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A is Noetherian, finite presentation = finite type. Motivation: 'finite in all possible ways' — finite generators, finite relations, finite cover by affines, intersections covered by finitely many affines. Characterization: locally finitely presented morphisms are exactly those that are limit-preserving for projective systems of affine Y-schemes (7.3.18). Exercises show affineness-local properties and closure under composition (7.3.T–W, U).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finite morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is quasi-finite if it is of finite type and for all y ∈ Y the fiber π^{-1}(y) is a finite set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key part is 'finite fiber'; finite morphisms are quasi-finite (combine Exercises 7.3.K and 7.3.P(a)). There are quasi-finite morphisms that are not finite (e.g., A^2 − {(0,0)} → A^2), but quasi-finite morphisms to Spec k are finite (Exercise 7.4.D). Visualization: quasi-finiteness is like a finite map with some closed locus of points removed (Zariski’s Main Theorem flavor; 7.3.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite = integral + finite type (criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is finite if and only if it is integral and of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Splits the property of finiteness into two checkable pieces (Exercise 7.3.P). Useful for proving finite-ness by checking integrality and finite-type hypotheses separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible subset (definition and criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructible subset of a Noetherian topological space is a member of the smallest family of subsets containing every open set and closed under finite intersections and complements. Equivalently in Noetherian spaces: finite disjoint unions of locally closed subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 7.4.A shows equivalence with finite disjoint unions of locally closed subsets. Useful facts: preimage of constructible under continuous maps is constructible; a constructible subset is closed iff stable under specialization (7.4.C(a)), open iff stable under generization (7.4.C(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley’s Theorem (image constructibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is a finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes, the image of any constructible set is constructible. In particular, the image of π is constructible (Theorem 7.4.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and uses: quick proof of the Nullstellensatz (3.2.5) (7.4.3); surjectivity of maps of varieties can be checked on closed points (7.4.E); proof uses Grothendieck's Generic Freeness Lemma and Noetherian induction (exercises 7.4.F–O). Extension to locally finitely presented morphisms is mentioned (9.3.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grothendieck’s Generic Freeness Lemma (property (†))
rubrics_metrics.description: If B is a Noetherian integral domain, then every finitely generated B-algebra satisfies property (†): for each finitely generated A-module M there exists a nonzero f ∈ B such that M_f is a free B_f-module (Lemma 7.4.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the proof of Chevalley. The text provides a sequence of exercises (7.4.F–K) that build the lemma: base case B itself (7.4.F), reduction to A[T] (7.4.G), and inductive module filtration arguments (7.4.H–K). Practical use: find a dense open over which fibers behave nicely (free of constant rank).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of quantifiers / constructibility of parameter conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given polynomials f_i and g_j in k[W1,..,Wm,X1,..,Xn] over an algebraically closed field k, there is a Zariski-constructible subset Y ⊂ k^m of parameter values such that the system f_i(...,X)=0 and g_j(...,X)≠0 has a solution in X iff the parameters lie in Y (Exercise 7.4.P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct algebraic formulation of existence of solutions as a constructible condition on coefficients, proved by forming the scheme X cut out by equalities/inequalities and applying Chevalley to the projection to parameter space. Analogy: Tarski's elimination for real closed fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory (projective maps are closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : P^n_A → Spec A the morphism is closed (sends closed sets to closed sets) (Theorem 7.4.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No Noetherian hypothesis needed. Classical consequences: determinants, resultants — one can write polynomial equations in coefficients that detect when homogeneous equations have a common nontrivial solution. Proof uses graded rings and linear algebra: non-surjectivity of certain maps SN−deg gi ⊕ ... → SN is a closed condition on coefficients (7.4.8 and Exercise 7.4.Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embedding / closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a closed embedding (closed immersion) if it is affine and for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) ≅ Spec A the map B → A is surjective (i.e., A ≅ B/I). If X is a subset of Y and π is set-theoretically inclusion, X is a closed subscheme of Y (Definition 8.1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: closed embeddings identify the topological space of X with a closed subset of Y (8.1.A), but the closed subset does not determine the closed subscheme (infinitesimal 'fuzz' can differ). Closed embeddings are finite and hence of finite type (8.1.B). Composition of closed embeddings is a closed embedding (8.1.C). Property is affine-local on the target (8.1.D). The kernel of O_Y → π_* O_X defines the ideal sheaf I_{X/Y} (8.1.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for gluing ideals to define a closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Given for each affine open Spec B ⊂ Y an ideal I(B) ⊂ B such that for each f ∈ B the natural map I(B)_f → I(B_f) is an isomorphism, then these ideals arise from a unique closed subscheme X ⊂ Y obtained by gluing the closed embeddings Spec B/I(B) → Spec B (Exercise 8.1.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a necessary and (this exercise shows) sufficient condition for local ideal data to define a global closed subscheme. The exercise is nontrivial; suggested approaches include checking compatibility on overlaps of affines and using sheaf/gluing arguments. Counterexamples (8.1.F) show naive data may fail if condition not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius morphism examples (behavioral criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: For k of characteristic p, the map φ(x_i) = x_i^p induces Frobenius morphisms with special properties: e.g., it can be the identity on underlying sets but not an isomorphism of schemes; it can be a bijection which is not an isomorphism (7.3.16–S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples serve as cautionary examples about geometric vs scheme-theoretic behavior of morphisms: bijectivity on points need not imply isomorphism; powers of Frobenius may fail to be identity on sets even when map is bijective. Useful in thinking about subtle distinctions when evaluating morphisms.
